kp.k: AI threatens revenue from tedious legal work
kp.d: Reporting on a 2026 American Bar Association White Collar Crime Institute panel, Jacob Shamsian attributes to Anthropic general counsel Jeff Bleich the prediction that AI will eliminate work that has made large teams of lawyers lucrative for firms. Bleich argues that this tedious work is not what lawyers are trained for or ultimately valued for. The report presents his expectation, rather than measured evidence of task elimination or lawyer displacement, and gives no specific implementation timeline.
qs: "Now we've got a technology that's going to eliminate the sorts of things that allow people to become wealthy off of tedious work," Bleich said on the panel, alongside top lawyers at Google, IBM, and Liberty Mutual.
"That was not what lawyers are trained to do, and not what we ultimately look to lawyers for."

kp.k: Hourly billing misaligns firms' and clients' incentives
kp.d: The article describes hourly billing as the standard law-firm charging method, often tracked in six-minute increments. Bleich acknowledges its usefulness in explaining charges but argues that it creates opposing incentives: clients seek quick, efficient resolution, whereas firms earn more from longer, more complicated matters. This incentive critique underpins his call to move beyond the billable hour.
qs: Attorneys track the work done for each client, often in six-minute increments, tally them up, and charge their clients accordingly.
"the interests of firms are at odds with the interests of their clients,"
"Clients want you to solve the problem as efficiently as possible and with as little drama as possible," Bleich said.
"I don't think the billable hour is the solution, and we've known it for a long time,"

kp.k: Corporate buyers emphasise strategy and results over time
kp.d: Liberty Mutual's top lawyer, Damon Hart, frames legal value as strategy and results rather than time spent. IBM general counsel Anne Robinson invites firms to negotiate more creative billing arrangements around expected outcomes and both parties' pressures and priorities. These are buyer-side preferences and invitations to collaborate, not evidence of an implemented pricing model or a specified fee formula.
qs: "The value is no longer you putting in time," said Damon Hart, the top lawyer at Liberty Mutual. "The value is your strategy, your results."

"I'm open to firms coming and saying, 'I'd really like to work with you on this matter or this type of work, I get that the billable hour model is not one of aligned incentives, and so let's sit down and talk about what you expect as far as outcomes and how we can both get there in a way that reflects your pressures and your priorities,'" Robinson said.

kp.k: Pricing adaptation could become a competitive advantage
kp.d: Bleich says he continues to value outside firms and wants an economically viable alternative to hourly billing, rather than simply cutting their compensation. He predicts that firms adapting faster and better will become more attractive to clients and overtake competitors. The competitive effect is his forecast, not a documented market outcome.
qs: Bleich said he still values the work of outside law firms, but wants them to find an alternative to the billable hour that works for everyone.
"We're not going to sort of cheap out and starve you," Bleich said.

"On the other hand, you have to have an economic model that works. And the firms that adapt to that faster and better will be leapfrogging other firms, because they'll be more attractive to work with."

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Bleich predicts that AI will eliminate lucrative tedious legal work and undermine hourly billing; corporate legal leaders favour paying for strategy and results instead.
pts.d: Jacob Shamsian frames the report as a prediction of the billable hour's approaching demise, attributing it to Anthropic general counsel Jeff Bleich. Bleich says AI will eliminate work from which lawyers have earned substantial revenues and argues that hourly billing misaligns law firms' incentives with clients' desire for efficient resolution. Liberty Mutual's Damon Hart describes strategy and results, rather than time spent, as the source of value. IBM general counsel Anne Robinson expresses willingness to negotiate outcome-oriented billing arrangements; this is a stated buyer preference, not evidence of an implemented pricing change. Bleich also predicts that firms adapting their economic models faster and better will become more attractive to clients and overtake competitors.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The claims rest on corporate legal leaders' testimony and incentive-based reasoning, not quantitative evidence of AI's effects.
pts.d: The report draws on remarks at the American Bar Association's White Collar Crime Institute from senior in-house lawyers, especially Bleich. Their positions provide a buyer-side perspective on desired changes to outside counsel billing. The causal argument is that AI removes time-consuming work while hourly billing rewards time spent rather than efficient outcomes. The supplied text offers no measured productivity gains, staffing reductions, billing-adoption statistics, model benchmarks, or documented AI-driven pricing transitions. Robinson's willingness to discuss alternative arrangements supports the existence of buyer interest, rather than demonstrating that hourly billing has already been displaced.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: AI disruption is presented as underway or imminent in the 2026 report, without a deadline for replacing hourly billing.
pts.d: Bleich's language presents the technology as available now and the elimination of tedious work as prospective. The report gives no date by which the billable hour will disappear or estimate of the pace or extent of change. Competitive gains are conditional on firms adapting faster and better than rivals. Bleich qualifies his pricing argument by affirming the continuing value of outside firms and the need for an economically sustainable model; he does not propose eliminating outside counsel or specify a single replacement fee structure.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The affected market is principally corporate clients purchasing outside legal services and the firms supplying them.
pts.d: Corporate legal departments are portrayed as wanting efficient problem resolution and billing aligned with outcomes. Outside law firms face pressure on revenues derived from tedious, time-intensive work and pressure to redesign pricing; early and effective adapters are predicted to gain a competitive advantage. Lawyers' strategic contributions and results remain valued. The article describes reduced need for large teams performing tedious work but does not quantify employment effects, identify particular seniority levels as displaced, or make claims about access to justice or individual-consumer legal services.
